posts.content_md: Well, I know this is unconventional for a display but I wanted a hologram that I could lay on the table and be able to view no matter what the illuminating souce angle was. So I tried an on axis Denisyk. I like the results. No matter how you turn the hologram the image is always visible. Dinesh, this may be something you want to consider for your coasters. Of couse the image cannot be too deep becaue of the slight smear but I got great results. The object was on a black surface and that produced too much cross talk. I will have to suspend the object further from the background. And of course the image slurres slightly as the replay light is off angle of the recoding angle (dead on) but the image is so nicely bright no matter how you rotate it, it may be a feature that superseeds the negative.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md: I seem to recall someone saying that coffee-table holos (Saxby's term) work better with a converging reference beam. I tried one recently with a (slightly) diverging beam and the results, while interesting, had too much perspective distortion to be acceptable. Ideally, for any holo the reference divergence should be the inverse (conjugate?) of the divergence of the replay light source, but usually a collimated beam is used with OK results. It could be that off axis distortions are much more obvious with coffee-table holos and so they might benefit from more careful matching of the divergences. Not sure how this would affect the brightness vs. viewing angle, though...

Thanks for the suggestion.

 In fact, I've had the idea for a "coffee table" hologram for many, many years. At the time, I was in a similar situation that I thought all these ideas were wonderfully innovative, only to find out that the same ideas were occurring to all new holographers. After a while, in holography gatherings like SPIE and Lake Forest, you start comparing your method for night lights, clocks, tables,dynamic game-playing chess boards etc, etc with everyone elses!

I was having dinner with Edwina and Dave (Richmond Holographics) and during the course of the dinner I mentioned how I always wanted a coffee table hologram. Well, Joy, being new to the game then (ca 1999) went into elaborate geometries. Dave and Edwina politely listened and then showed us one they'd made some 10 years previously and said, "Like this?" 

In fact some of our desk holograms are designed to be viewed while on a desk by someone sitting and viewing them from a height of about 1.5 feet. I figured the average person has a eye-to-hand distance while writing of about 18" - 24" and the hologram centre is about 3", thus the hologram should be viewed from about 15" to 21" above it.

posts.content_md: So is there some trick to making better CT holos? (other than using shallow objects close to the plate) Is a converging beam helpful?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:92ad973cc7="Tom B."]I seem to recall someone saying that coffee-table holos (Saxby's term) work better with a converging reference beam. I tried one recently with a (slightly) diverging beam and the results, while interesting, had too much perspective distortion to be acceptable. Ideally, for any holo the reference divergence should be the inverse (conjugate?) of the divergence of the replay light source, but usually a collimated beam is used with OK results. It could be that off axis distortions are much more obvious with coffee-table holos and so they might benefit from more careful matching of the divergences. Not sure how this would affect the brightness vs. viewing angle, though...[/quote:92ad973cc7]

As always, you need to think backwards to the lighting that's going to reconstruct the hologram. You're right that the reference should be the conjugate of the reconstruction and usually a collimated beam works and is easy to set up. However, the larger the hologram, the greater the distortions, or rather, the more the distortiomns are noticed.. So while a hologram on a 4x5 is pretty forgiving for a reasonable reconstruction mismatch, you need to be more accurate for a coffee table hologram of typical coffee table dimensions, say 48" x 20" odd. It also depends on the depth of the hologram. Most aberrations start at the plate and distort the image more as the depth gets greater, so the deeper the hologram, the more the effects of reference mismatch. However, having said that, it depends a lot on the image. The image I saw at Richmond was potted plants apparently set underneath the glass of the table. In this case, you had seperate images, each of which was small compared to the overall size of the hologram. Thus any small distortion in each image element (a single potted plant) would be small.
